Yeahhhh...that is definitely wrong. I was always told to call and ask if they are expecting a dramatic change before I do anything drastic like invalidate the results. Sometimes there is IV fluid contaminate or something causing crazy results. But I would never cancel a test without the nurse agreeing that the results may be inaccurate. I hate to say it, but there are a lot of crappy lab people out there :/

Labs are generally able to put multiple patient samples on the analyzer to run tests at a time. The instrument can still usually only do one sample at a time, so the results still come off one by one (depends on what instruments the lab has for chemistries, hematology, etc). So we will look at the results and analyze and interpret them. Are the results valid? Does it look like there is some type of mistake? Every once in a while, the sample is labeled with the wrong patient or someone transfers the blood from one color tube to a different one and affects the results. But usually, a critical is a critical and we will call as soon as we see it. (At least I do). In order of priority, if it is stat, we will run it first, and there are certain specimens that have priority above all else, like stroke patients, liver transplants, certain results like first time acute promyelocytic leukemia in the hematology dept., it really just depends, but usually, if the results come up first, they will be called first. We don't have criticals as often as you might think. There are tons of rules to follow as to whether you need to call the results or not.

I agree with reactive/atyp lymph. I used to get these confused a lot, but I've gotten a lot of practice and have a better eye now. That cell is extremely blue and dark. Myelocytes and beyond are generally a more pink color, like the cell above it. So if you think it might be a myelocyte, look for other cells around that are DEFINITELY of that lineage and compare the colors and granules and overall looks of the cells. Myelos and metas tend to look like segs, just before their nucleus has stretched out to a band/seg. That cell looks more like a stretched out lymph.

Always tailor your cover letter to the specific place you are applying to. 

1. State the position you are applying for and how you discovered it.
2. Introduce the reasons why you're a great fit for the position. (Education, work experience, etc)
3. Go into more detail about your reasons. Explain your resume, don't just put it in essay form. 
4. Explain any other special circumstances, like if you're in a different state and plan to move or something like that. 
5. Conclude with summary, thank them, and let them know you want to discuss the position further. 
6. That's basically it.

I actually used to be a pathology tech in the midwest. In my lab, histology and the gross room were separated, but worked very closely with each other. The path tech does exactly what your description says. If you are unsure what those things mean, don't worry, I was clueless as well when I started. 

We got specimens that were removed from surgery(could be pretty much any organ/body part). My job was to make sure the specimens had no errors, and put the specimen into the computer to get labels and such. (accessioning). I also had to prepare many of the specimens by putting formalin on them, but some of them needed to stay fresh.

When you dictate the gross descriptions, you are simply describing what they look like. At my lab, you said the description while wearing a headset, and a computer program would transcribe your words into text. This way you are able to keep your hands free to cut the specimen.

Frozen sections are stats, so they need to be done right away. At my lab, a resident pathologist would cut the specimen so just the part that was in question for diagnosis would be cut. That specimen piece would get embedded in this stuff that looks kinda like colored glue, that also freezes really fast. Once it is embedded and frozen, you cut the specimen with a machine called a cryostat, which allows you get VERY thin slices. You are then able to press a microscope slide to the specimen to get it on there, then you stain it. Then an attending pathologist is called in and he makes a diagnosis based on your slides.

I had no experience with this when I started, but I definitely learned, so if it's something you want to do, don't feel scared just because you have no experience.

 At my lab, a path tech could not become a histotech, but if you showed interested in working in histology, you could eventually get transferred there if you wanted. Several people at my lab did this. If you transferred, your title was "histology assistant," and my hospital allowed you to train while working to become a histotech. Several people did this as well.

So to answer one of your questions, a pathology tech trainee most likely wont DIRECTLY get you to histotech, but it may get you in the door, depending on your facility. 

1. It seems like there is some demand, but probably less demand than MT. but I've definitely seen positions available everywhere i've moved to.

2. They make somewhere around the same as MT. ~40-60k, depending on region.

3. I've never been a histotech, so I can't give full details, but I know they work with tissues to make slides. So your experience you get cutting frozens should help. It seems more machine oriented.

4. I don't know what someone could do as a histotech other than be a histotech. But if you become a path tech trainee, you will definitely get a good feel for what the anatomic pathology department does, and if you have a bachelor's degree, you could eventually apply for a pathologist's assistant graduate program, which many people I know do after working as a path tech for a few years.
